title: IUMS upper limb · 1399/11/08 · 25-question paper
note: IUMS online examination screenshots dated 1399/11/08 on the cover; not a confirmed TUMS final. Three overlapping downloads are one paper, with the photographed answer grid retained as supplied (not authenticated official) evidence. Cover screenshots contain a student's name, so originals stay in the private archive. Full includes limb-development and vertebral items; Upper only excludes these. Two defective questions remain in the source download without a score.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true for the radial nerve?
options: Injury to the radial nerve causes numbness in the dorsal skin of the lateral 3.5 fingers.
The nerve to the lateral head of triceps innervates anconeus.
The nerve to the posterior skin of the forearm separates after the radial groove.
The nerve to brachialis separates inside the radial groove.
questions.note: A is the intended supplied answer, but its sensory territory excludes the distal dorsal fingertips/nail beds, which are largely median supplied. The radial nerve supplies proximal dorsal lateral digits. The anconeus branch accompanies the medial-head branch; posterior forearm cutaneous branches arise in the groove, while the brachialis branch is distal to it.

questions.prompt: If interdigital apoptosis stops in a growing limb, which change is expected?
options: Proximal-distal patterning does not occur normally.
Bones and muscles do not form.
The digits remain connected and do not separate.
questions.note: Failure of interdigital programmed cell death can cause soft-tissue syndactyly. This does not imply that all bone formation or proximodistal patterning ceases.

questions.prompt: Damage to which peripheral nerve(s) would impair pronation of the forearm?
questions.note: The intended pair D identifies pronator teres supply via median nerve and pronator quadratus via its AIN branch. Because the original says impair rather than abolish, an isolated AIN lesion or proximal median lesion can also impair pronation: A, C and D are accepted. 'External pronation' in the source is not a standard movement term.

questions.prompt: If intrinsic hand motor function and sensation in the fifth digit and ulnar half of the fourth digit are lost, where is the ulnar nerve damaged?
questions.note: The supplied grid marks A, but the findings do not uniquely localize a lesion. A proximal ulnar lesion at the elbow or before Guyon's canal can cause both deficits; distal canal involvement depends on branching level and which sensory surfaces are affected. No forearm motor or dorsal-hand sensory findings are supplied. Retained ungraded rather than teaching a false unique level.

questions.prompt: A 10-year-old fractures the humeral surgical neck. Which finding is not expected from the associated axillary nerve injury?

questions.note: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and the upper lateral arm patch, not upper medial arm skin. Deltoid atrophy is a later sign, not an immediate post-fracture finding. The source's 'could not be checked' wording is clarified to the nerve territory being tested.

questions.prompt: Which can occur after injury to the lower roots of the brachial plexus?
questions.note: Lower plexus C8-T1 injury is termed Klumpke palsy and can produce clawing; A and C are accepted for the nonexclusive source wording. questions.prompt: Resegmentation of the vertebrae does not cause which event?
options: Intersegmental arteries lie opposite the middle of vertebral bodies.
A vertebra forms from adjacent caudal and cranial sclerotome portions.
Formation of primary thoracic and sacral curvatures.
questions.note: Resegmentation joins the caudal half of one sclerotome to the cranial half of the next, permitting segmental muscle bridges and repositioning the arterial relationship. Primary spinal curvatures are not caused by resegmentation.
